options: A scheduling practice that splits shifts between two or more employees
A requirement that passwords be split between two people
A rule requiring every employee to work in exactly one department
The principle that no single person should hold two permissions that combined enable fraud or serious error on their own
questions.explain: SoD is a structural control: if one person can both initiate and approve an action, there's no independent review of it.

questions.q: What makes a 'toxic combination' different from simply having 'too much access'?
options: A toxic combination always involves more than five permissions at once
Toxic combinations only apply to IT administrator accounts
There is no real difference — the two terms mean exactly the same thing
The danger exists specifically in the pairing of two permissions — neither permission is necessarily risky on its own
questions.explain: Create Vendor and Approve Payment are each harmless alone; the risk is created only when one person holds both.

questions.q: In the classic create-vendor/approve-payment toxic combination, how does the fraud actually work?
options: One person creates a vendor record and then approves a payment to it themselves, with no one else reviewing the transaction
The fraud requires access to the HR system, not the ERP
The ERP system automatically pays any vendor added to its database
Two separate employees must collude over email to commit the fraud
questions.explain: Holding both permissions lets one person invent a vendor and approve payment to it unilaterally — a complete fraud cycle with zero external review.

questions.q: Why does granting access and certifying that same access count as a toxic combination for an IT administrator?
options: It causes the access certification software to crash
Certification campaigns do not apply to IT staff at all
It removes the independent check that an access certification campaign is supposed to provide
IT administrators are never allowed to grant access under any circumstances
questions.explain: If the person who grants access is also the one who certifies it's appropriate, there's no second set of eyes — the same structural flaw as any other toxic combination.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say SoD must be checked across a person's total access, not within just one system?
options: Cross-system access is impossible to review in any identity program
A toxic combination can span two systems — e.g., approve-payment rights in the ERP plus a separate database login that bypasses the ERP's own controls
Checking within a single system is always sufficient and faster
Only cloud-based systems need to be checked for SoD violations
questions.explain: A single application's permission list won't show a combination that's split across two different systems, even though the same person still holds both halves of it.
